items.title: OpenAI seeks to accelerate fundraising ahead of Anthropic IPO, sources say: Reuters exclusive
items.description: OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, according to two sources.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[Open AI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference, Tuesday, Sept. 29, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Jeff Chiu</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, according to two sources.
items.body:
OpenAI is racing to secure investor commitments before rival Anthropic’s expected public market debut in mid-November, in an unusually fast fundraising that could value the ChatGPT maker at over US$1.4 trillion, according to two people familiar with the matter.

The rapid timetable reflects, in part, a desire to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are increasingly tapping in to a similar investor base, the people said, adding that OpenAI wants to capitalize on its recent revenue growth after launching new models. SoftBank Group, Abu Dhabi-based MGX and other existing backers of OpenAI are in talks to join the round of about US$30 billion, one of the people said.

The acceleration underscores how closely the two AI developers are competing for capital as both pursue trillion-dollar price tags, amid growing concern about rising interest rates, significant volatility in technology stocks and rising scrutiny of AI valuations.

  • Latest updates on company news here

OpenAI held meetings with long-only funds and sovereign wealth funds last week while Anthropic was hosting its own investor day. OpenAI’s funding round is expected to move faster than is typical for an offering of its size, the people said.

Investors familiar with the company say OpenAI also needs capital to fund its substantial infrastructure commitments and bolster its balance sheet if a deterioration in the IPO markets further delays its planned 2027 listing.

Though there is high demand for the shares of both companies, investors face the challenge of evaluating and allocating capital to two complex, competing offerings within days or weeks of each other. Some investors view OpenAI’s financing push as an effort to lock in capital from funds that might otherwise devote more of their resources to Anthropic’s IPO, the people said.

OpenAI and SoftBank declined to comment. Anthropic and MGX did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Trying to head off comparisons

OpenAI is pitching investors on growth that accelerated after the launch of its GPT-6 Astra model, saying it had reached US$50 billion in annualized revenue and expecting that figure to rise to US$70 billion by year-end, according to one of the people.

OpenAI has also cut prices on its cheaper models, which it said has boosted usage, and told investors it can further lower the price of AI models, the person added.

Anthropic’s annualized revenue reached roughly US$65 billion by July, Reuters previously reported. Its quarterly revenue jumped to US$16.8 billion in the third quarter from US$11.6 billion in the second quarter this year, it told investors, but slowing month-to-month revenue growth has raised concerns among investors about its valuation.

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

OpenAI is seeking to complete the fundraising before Anthropic’s financial disclosures give investors a fuller picture of its business and invite comparisons between the two companies, one person said.

The disclosures could prompt investors to press OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar for more details about the company’s revenue growth and financial outlook, the person added. OpenAI records revenue on a net basis by subtracting partner shares upfront. It has accused Anthropic of inflating its revenue by counting the full, gross value of contracts sold through third-party cloud providers. Anthropic told Reuters earlier that it follows established accounting practices.

“OpenAI could want to set its own valuation and not have to worry about a comp (comparison),” said Edward Best, co-chair of capital markets at Willkie Farr & Gallagher, who is not working on the deal and commented on a hypothetical basis. “It’s really a two-horse race in terms of being public.”

OpenAI was last valued at US$852 billion in March this year, after a record-breaking US$122 billion funding round, including a commitment from Amazon.com AMZN.O, which agreed to invest up to US$50 billion in the lab.

The Financial Times previously reported some details of OpenAI’s potential fundraising.

IPO plans hit by market jitters

A number of companies preparing to go public have decided to wait until after Anthropic’s planned IPO, wary of competing for investor demand amid market volatility and a pullback in AI stocks, bankers and investors said. Some late-stage companies are also timing private fundraising rounds to avoid coinciding with Anthropic’s expected debut, the bankers and investors said.

Some existing and prospective Anthropic investors have argued for a valuation closer to US$1.5 trillion for its market debut — instead of the desired US$2 trillion — after the AI startup’s third-quarter results fell short of expectations, Reuters reported last week.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

The reassessment comes amid a choppy market since September, with volatility in oil prices, rising bond yields and growing concerns about AI safety weighing on investor appetite for technology stocks. Investors are also scrutinizing the cost of AI infrastructure, including the debt needed to finance the data centers powering the boom.

At the center of the latest concerns is cloud provider CoreWeave, whose shares and debt tumbled last week as investors scrutinized the nearly US$50 billion in borrowings used to fund its rapid expansion.

The uncertainty has disrupted what had been expected to be a busy autumn for IPOs, with companies reassessing their listing plans amid market volatility and concerns about valuations. Blackstone-backed AirTrunk REIT, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either pulled or paused their listings.

Nuclear services company Holtec cited a “perfect storm,” driven mainly by uncertainty around data-center demand, ​when it pulled its US listing last month.

Companies in the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, widely viewed as a proxy for AI-related semiconductor demand, have shed US$1.6 trillion in less than two weeks, while AI infrastructure companies have come under particular pressure.

Reporting by Echo Wang and Sabrina Valle in New York and Krystal Hu in San Francisco; Editing by Colin Barr and Matthew Lewis

items.title: China defends DeepSeek after U.S. ban of its AI from government systems
items.description: China hit back at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products by federal civilian agencies.

items._ogDesc: China hit back at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products by federal civilian agencies.
items.body:
HONG KONG — China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products by federal civilian agencies and warned of retaliatory measures as the two AI powers race to develop the technology.

The Department of Homeland Security said the agencies should remove DeepSeek products as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek from their IT systems, according to a notice made public on Monday.

The latest warnings reflect “the depth of strategic distrust between Beijing and Washington” even as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping work hard to keep their personal relationship “warm and constructive,” said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at Washington-based The Asia Group consultancy.

  • Latest updates on international news here

The Homeland Security order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services.

DeepSeek’s open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States, and are mostly free to use.

The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” Concerns include that DeepSeek’s servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data, the order says.

Asked in Beijing about the U.S. ban, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies.”

  • Latest updates on artificial intelligence news here

“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security,” she told reporters.

China’s Ministry of Commerce also expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” against the U.S.’s move, saying late Tuesday that the U.S. side disregarded the consensus reached between Xi and Trump and ignored the broader landscape of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.

Through discriminatory restrictions under “the guise of national security,” the U.S. is trying to suppress and contain China, the commerce ministry statement said. “China will closely monitor the situation and take all necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”

DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up a notification system on national security-related incidents, but they remain at odds on many issues.

AI is expected to be on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet again in mid-November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The two leaders last met in September as Xi made a state visit to Washington.

U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them.

The U.S. also has said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek had engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.

And last week, Beijing rolled out its own proposals to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.

Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

items.title: GSMA urges ‘policy reset’ for Canada’s telecom sector
items.description: A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions to invest.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[A person holds a smartphone in this stock image. (Shutterstock)]]></media:description>
items._ogDesc: A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions to invest.
items.body:
TORONTO — A new report says the focus of Canada’s telecommunications policy should shift from lowering consumer prices to creating better conditions for companies to invest in their networks at a time when traditional revenues are plateauing and capital costs are on the rise.

The paper from U.K.-based Global System for Mobile Communications calls for a “policy reset” that prioritizes affordable and predictable spectrum pricing, support for 5G and AI infrastructure such as data centres, and improved regulatory certainty.

It says mobile technologies and services generated 5.4 per cent of Canada’s GDP last year, or roughly $120 billion of economic value — a figure expected to rise to $170 billion by 2030, thanks to growing adoption of technologies such as 5G, Internet of Things and AI.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

In recent years, the CRTC has introduced various measures aimed at boosting cellphone and internet competition in Canada, empowering consumers, and lowering costs.

But without a policy shift, the report warns that network quality and innovation could gradually weaken.

It points to challenges facing telecom operators in Canada such as fewer new subscribers because of slower immigration, flat revenues and the rising cost of spectrum licences.

The Global System for Mobile Communications is an organization representing mobile operators worldwide. This is its first Canadian policy report.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The U.S. stock market is rising following reports showing strong profits for Equifax, Hasbro and other companies during the summer, while oil prices eased.
items.body:
NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market is rising Tuesday following reports showing strong profits for Equifax, Hasbro and other companies during the summer, while oil prices eased back after nearing their highest levels since the war with Iran began.

The S&P 500 climbed 0.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 667 points, or 1.3 per cent, as of 10:45 a.m. Eastern time, while more swings for the artificial-intelligence industry had the Nasdaq composite up a more modest 0.5 per cent.

Stock prices tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, and several companies delivered results for the latest quarter that were higher than analysts expected. Big expectations for growth generally are what have allowed the U.S. stock market to hit records recently despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.

  • S&P 500 market updates here

Equifax rallied 10.7 per cent for one of the market’s biggest gains after reporting a bigger profit for the summer than analysts expected, despite high mortgage rates slowing some parts of its business.

Hasbro climbed 5.9 per cent after the toy company said its “Magic: The Gathering” game made more than US$600 million during a quarter for the first time, even as shoppers broadly feel discouraged by high inflation. Hasbro’s overall profit blew past analysts’ expectations, and it raised its forecasts for revenue growth and an important measure of profitability this year.

Halliburton added 0.8 per cent after reporting profit and revenue that were bigger than analysts expected. CEO Jeff Miller said that the work to restore production and rebuild inventories following “one of the largest energy disruptions in history” will drive demand for its oilfield services.

In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude erased an early gain to fall 2.5 per cent to US$106.78. Earlier in the morning, it got near US$112 and approached its highest price since the war with Iran began in late February.

The drop in oil prices helped all kinds of stocks and will relieve some of the pressure on inflation if it lasts. Brent’s price has been yo-yoing between US$97 and US$112 per barrel this month on uncertainty about when the energy industry will return to normal.

  • Stay on top of your portfolio with real-time data, historical charts and the latest news on oil

For now, airlines and other companies with big fuel bills enjoyed the benefit of Tuesday’s drop. American Airlines jumped 7.1 per cent, and United Airlines flew 5.3 per cent higher.

Another winner was Braze, a customer engagement platform. Its stock soared 50.8 per cent to US$45.30 after Salesforce said it would buy the company for US$47.50 in cash for each share. Salesforce fell 0.8 per cent.

Keeping the market in check was General Motors, which sank 4.9 per cent despite reporting a bigger profit than analysts expected. It also announced a program to send up to US$20 billion to investors by buying back its stock.

The pressure is on companies to deliver bigger profits not only now, but also in the future. GM gave a forecasted range for profit over the full year of 2026 whose midpoint fell short of analysts’ expectations.

AI stocks, meanwhile, continued to swirl. They’ve been at the center of the market’s recent uneasiness, as euphoria around the technology’s boom gives way to worries that high interest rates in the bond market will slow the borrowing that’s allowed companies to buy so many AI chips. Last week was the U.S. stock market’s worst since June.

CoreWeave has been particularly shaky. It initially fell more than 6 per cent at the start of Tuesday’s trading, only to swing to a gain of 4.1 per cent.

Such reversals are nothing new for the company, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 7 per cent in the morning and a loss of 3.5 per cent in the afternoon following last week’s tumble of roughly 25 per cent.

  • Latest technology news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Tuesday’s struggles for AI stocks began in Asia, where a South Korean AI company, Elice, confronted a rough welcome to the stock market. Its stock dropped 32 per cent in its first day of trading in Seoul. South Korea’s Kospi index fell 3.7 per cent overall.

In other stock markets abroad, indexes in Europe pared early losses. The CAC 40 in Paris slipped 0.1 per cent, and the FTSE 100 in London fell 0.2 per cent.

A day earlier, indexes fell sharply across Europe following violent protests that could ultimately force governments on the continent to increase their spending to ease voters’ anger. That in turn could put more pressure on their bond markets, which are already strained because of worries about heavy debt loads and strained budgets.

Stan Choe, The Associated Press

AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

items.title: Gimmick or giveback? Even some Trump supporters don’t expect to get US$5,000 cheques after midterms
items.description: U.S. President Donald Trump is hoping that US$5,000 cheques can juice Republican turnout in November’s midterm elections — but even some of his devoted fans are doubting that government payouts would arrive.
items.content: <media:description type="plain"><![CDATA[President Donald Trump greets supporters as he arrives to speak at the Republican convention, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson, File)]]></media:description><media:credit role="author" scheme="urn:ebu">Julia Demaree Nikhinson</media:credit>
items._ogDesc: U.S. President Donald Trump is hoping that US$5,000 cheques can juice Republican turnout in November’s midterm elections — but even some of his devoted fans are doubting that government payouts would arrive.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump is hoping that US$5,000 cheques can juice Republican turnout in November’s midterm elections — but even some of his devoted fans are doubting that government payouts would arrive.

“I mean, I guess it’s good for some people. I really don’t care,” said Jamie Alvarez, who attended Trump’s recent Alaska rally in a red, white and blue outfit. ”I don’t feel like your vote should be bought. I feel like you should vote for who you feel is going to do the best job.”

Joseph Eatherton was attending that same rally and said he was “not sure if it’s necessary.” When asked whether Trump could deliver on the promised money, he said, “I don’t know, and I hate being an armchair quarterback.”

The offering of government cheques has become a go-to tactic for Trump when he faces a political jam. He’s previously endorsed $2,000 in dividends from tariff revenues and large refunds from spending cuts achieved by the Department of Government Efficiency, neither of which materialized. The latest example could reveal how much voters still trust Trump as they decide control of Congress in the midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Staunch supporters such as Lucy Martinez, the president of a Republican women’s club who attended a recent Trump rally in Texas, said there’s no doubt in their minds.

“I think that I will get the $5,000,” she said. Out of all the presidents, Trump is someone “who kept his promises to his people and all the United States.”

Trump has dished out payments as elections approach

However, many voters are already embittered by his economic leadership. His critics see a president who failed to tame inflation and keep America out of overseas conflicts, and whose agenda has fueled higher prices as the war with Iran appears to be at a stalemate.

“The trust on this is already gone for most people,” said Amy Frederiksen, a former Republican Minnesota Senate majority leader who now runs a public affairs firm.

“I just don’t see the energy around that line,” she added. “Most people know that’s a blatant over-the-top promise like several he’s made in the last couple of years, and they’re not buying it.”

As the midterms approach, Trump has also pledged a $90 payment to 20 million Medicare enrollees and $500 “rebates” for people the administration says were overcharged for their Obamacare plans. He has automatically enrolled every U.S. child in “Trump accounts” to invest in stocks.

The $5,000 payouts would only occur, Trump says, if Republicans keep their majorities in the House and Senate. Trump acknowledges that the cost would exceed $1 trillion, but it’s not clear that the White House is seriously engaging with the proposal’s ramifications, from the increased deficit to the likely boost to inflation.

The White House said the payments are possible because of Trump’s trade deals, investment commitments by foreign countries, government stakes in private companies and deals for oil and minerals.

The administration’s position is that the payments will help people recover from the inflation that began in 2021 under then-President Joe Biden, though Republicans, at the time, attributed that inflation to excessive government checks tied to pandemic relief.

When The Associated Press asked several weeks ago if the administration was modeling the economic impact from the checks, Christopher Phelan, chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers, said he would “refrain” from answering.

Roughly half of registered voters say Donald Trump does not keep his promises to Americans, according to an AP-NORC poll from September. About 3 in 10 say Trump tries to keep his promises but is unable to, while only about 2 in 10 say he keeps his promises.

Republican voters are more accommodating. About half say Trump tries to keep his promises but is unable to, and about 4 in 10 say he keeps his promises.

Republican candidates aren’t echoing Trump’s promise

Trump is talking about the payments as a sure thing.

“If the Republicans win, you’ll each have $5,000 in your pocket and economic success for our country like we have never seen before,” he said at a Saturday rally in Kentucky. “And remember, ’cause they like to say, ‘Oh, well, maybe he won’t do that.’ Uh, I always do it.”

Campaign spending tracked by AdImpact suggests that Republicans are not running advertisements either on television or online about the promise. The few advertisements that do exist are from pro-Democratic groups such as Rolling Sea Action Fund that conclude with the voiceover, “Come on, do you really think he’s sending you a check? Yeah, right, we won’t get fooled again.”

At a Friday rally in Georgia, Trump noted that he had previously delivered a $1,776 “Trump dividend” to troops in the military. But those payments came from a congressionally approved housing supplement.

Trump claims the nation could not afford the payments if Democrats hold a chamber in Congress because the nation would be “flat broke.” But he said that one caveat is that the money could only be spent in the U.S., rather than in China, Japan or France. He joked that people should spend the check at his luxury club in Palm Beach, Florida.

“Let’s have lunch at Mar-a-Lago, where for $5,000, you’ll get one hamburger and a small dessert,” he told the crowd in Georgia.

Some in the crowd took Trump at his word that he would fight to get them the money. But they added the caveat that if he didn’t come through, it would not be his fault.

“I could use $5,000,” said Mike Boatman, a 58-year-old from Evansville, Indiana, who travels the country attending the president’s rallies. “I mean, he’s done everything he’s said he’s going to do.”

Josh Boak, Becky Bohrer and Bill Barrow, The Associated Press

Bohrer reported from Wasilla, Alaska, and Barrow reported from Dalton, Georgia. Associated Press reporters Aaron Kessler and Linley Sanders in Washington and Lekan Oyekanmi in San Antonio, Texas, contributed.

items.title: Trump and Vance to announce a US$25M whistleblower program to encourage public to report alleged fraud
items.description: The Trump administration is set to announce a US$25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government.

items._ogDesc: The Trump administration is set to announce a US$25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government.
items.body:
WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump and U.S. Vice President JD Vance are set Tuesday to announce a US$25 million program to encourage the public to blow the whistle on suspected fraud in the federal government as they ramp up an existing effort to end the abuse of federal programs and dollars.

Under the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, or WHIP, anyone who submits a tip to fraud.gov that leads to a fraud conviction or a significant federal enforcement action is eligible to receive up to US$30,000, the White House said. The Justice Department will administer the program.

The Republican president has undertaken an aggressive effort to eliminate fraud throughout the government. Trump established a task force on the topic in March and put Vance in charge of it.

  • Latest updates on international news here

They are scheduled to announce the fund during a joint appearance in the Oval Office later Tuesday.

“Every day, President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud is zeroing in on the rampant abuse of taxpayer dollars and giving Americans the accountability they deserve. This administration has zero tolerance for individuals who steal from Americans,” said White House spokesperson Lauren Bis.

During the Oval Office event, Trump will present a US$10,000 check to Nick Shirley, a right-wing influencer who posted a video last year that said members of Minnesota’s Somali community were running fake childcare centers to collect federal subsidies.

The video caught the attention of the Trump administration and conservative activists, though inspectors said the centers were operating as expected. Investigations, searches and arrests followed.

In July, one woman, Fahima Mahamud, pleaded guilty to wire fraud and conspiracy to defraud the United States by submitting inflated reimbursement claims for meals allegedly served to children at her childcare center, according to the Justice Department.

The White House says Mahamud was featured in Shirley’s video.

Darlene Superville, The Associated Press

Albertans rejected holding a second referendum to separate as voters overwhelmingly chose to stay in Canada, CTV News projects.

In a historic vote that saw the oil-rich province put the question of separation to the public, roughly 75 per cent of voters thought Alberta should stay in Canada, while just under 25 per cent voted to pursue a binding referendum on leaving, according to preliminary results just after 8 a.m. MT.

The remaining nine questions, focused largely on immigration and constitutional changes, are also being counted right now and some have close races.

The emphatic result to remain culminates a year-long campaign from pro-Canada and separatist groups.

The Alberta government, on the other hand, campaigned for yes votes on the first nine questions, and Premier Danielle Smith also advocated for the province to remain in Canada.

She will address Albertans at 6:45 p.m. MT on Tuesday.

Elections Alberta was expected to announce results for Question 10 by 4 a.m. MT, but not all polls are reporting results yet.

Results for the first nine questions will be announced Wednesday morning.

items.body:
OTTAWA — The Parliamentary Budget Office is trimming its outlook for economic growth for this year and next amid new U.S. tariffs and Canadian countermeasures.

The federal budget watchdog says it now projects real gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

The forecast is down from an estimate in June for growth of 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively.

  • Latest economic news on BNNBloomberg.ca

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down at the end of August followed by a new round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.

The PBO says it also now projects a budgetary deficit of $63.3 billion for the 2026-27 fiscal year which will peak at $70.2 billion in 2027-28.

It says, relative to its June outlook, the deficits are $3 billion higher per year on average over 2026‑27 to 2030‑31, as new spending measures more than offset stronger revenues.

items._ogDesc: Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London were disrupted by a Google Cloud outage Tuesday.
items.body:
LONDON — Online services for a number of U.K. banks in and around London were disrupted by a Google Cloud outage Tuesday.

The cloud outages began just after 2 a.m. eastern, or 6:08 a.m. GMT.

The center of the outage is London, but the impact can extend outside of the U.K. if apps in other countries rely on London-based infrastructure.

“Our engineering team continues to investigate the issue,” Google Cloud said early Tuesday. It said that it was starting to see a recovery of services.

U.K. banks that reported disruptions include Lloyds, Halifax, HSBC and Revolut.

“We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services,” Revolut said in an email. ”We can confirm that all our customers’ money and data are safe. We’ve been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused.”

Lloyds said its app is again operational.

“We understand the root issues have been resolved, so we expect to all our services to be back to normal soon,” a Lloyds spokesperson said in an email.

There appear to be outages elsewhere in Europe, but it is unclear if they are connected.

“We apologize to all who are affected by the disruption,” Google Cloud said.

items.body:
MUMBAI, India — U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio held talks with India’s foreign minister in Mumbai on Tuesday as the two countries seek to deepen energy cooperation and move closer to finalizing a trade deal.

India and the United States seek to revive trade negotiations stalled for months by tensions over American tariffs and the Indian government’s purchases of Russian oil.

“We’re very, very close. I would say we’re about as close as you can be without having executed the agreement,” Rubio told reporters in Mumbai on Tuesday. “I think there’s a small number of items left to wrap up, so I think that will happen shortly.”

  • Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.ca

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said that they discussed ways to strengthen bilateral ties in trade, energy, technology and defense, along with talks on regional developments.

Jaishankar and Rubio also held a trilateral meeting with United Arab Emirates Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, who also was visiting India. Rubio said that the three officials met to discuss “regional energy security and advance our shared economic priorities.”

Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50 per cent on most Indian goods in August 2025 after trade talks broke down. Under a framework agreed upon in February, the tariff rate was reduced to 18 per cent, but the negotiations have since stalled.

Earlier this month, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said that the talks had “plateaued.” Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal, however, said last week that the first tranche of a trade deal was in its final stages.

India says its final tariff rate should be similar to those of competing manufacturing countries such as Vietnam.

India’s purchases of discounted Russian crude since the start of the war in Ukraine in February 2022 have strained ties with the United States at times. The Indian government has said that it would expand energy imports, including from the U.S., while diversifying suppliers to maintain market stability and keep prices affordable.

Despite tensions, the two countries continue to deepen defense and technology ties, with Washington viewing India as a key counterweight to China in the Indo-Pacific.

Rubio’s visit to India follows a trip to Uzbekistan this week to promote trade and ties with Central Asia.

Rubio told reporters in the United States on Saturday before his departure that India had diversified its energy sources, but continued to buy substantial volumes of Russian oil, making an immediate shift to other suppliers difficult.

“You’ve got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it’s hard to pivot from one day to the next,” he said. “But they’re also an important ally and partner of the United States.”

Rubio is scheduled to visit a refinery in the city of Jamnagar in Gujarat state on Wednesday and meet with business leaders, according to the U.S. State Department.

The Jamnagar facility, operated by Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is the world’s largest refining complex. In March, U.S. President Donald Trump announced that the company was investing US$300 billion to set up an oil refinery in Brownsville, Texas.

items.title: Canada’s Approved-But-Unstarted Homes Climb As Starts Slide
items.description:
Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) counted 143,929 homes in September that have approved building permits and no construction started.

That count, reported alongside CMHC’s figures for centres of 50,000 or more, rose 1.1% from August.

Compared with a year ago, starts have fallen. Actual housing starts in centres of 10,000 or more were down 11% year-over-year in September, at 19,984 units compared with 22,375. From January through September, those centres recorded 170,964 starts, 4% behind the same period in 2025.

“As outlined in CMHC’s latest Housing Supply Report (HSR), a key risk for Canada now is not building enough during this period of softening housing markets across the country,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at CMHC.

“Canada still faces a long-term housing supply gap and unless housing construction levels increase, improvements in housing affordability since 2023 will be difficult to sustain,” he said.

In ab Iorwerth’s view, the affordability relief since 2023 will be hard to keep without more building. Right now, starts are down from last year.

The headline figures make that harder to see: the seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) of starts across Canada rose 3% in September, to 248,896 units from 242,223 in August. CMHC’s six-month trend, a moving average of that rate, barely budged, and landed at 250,411.

CMHC uses the trend alongside the monthly SAAR to account for considerable swings in the monthly figure. Multi-unit starts largely drive the market, and they can vary widely from one month to the next.

Homes already underway are holding steady. There were 371,617 units under construction in centres of 50,000 or more in September, flat from August. Completions fell 0.9% to 17,398 units.

The regional picture is uneven. “Of Canada’s four most populous provinces, only Quebec has seen modest gains in housing starts for 2026 and each of the seven major centres covered in the HSR are behind 2025’s pace for new home construction,” ab Iorwerth said.

Montreal’s six-month trend fell 8% in September on lower multi-unit starts. Vancouver’s rose 6% on higher multi-unit starts. Toronto’s was flat, with single-detached and multi-unit trends offsetting each other.

CMHC will release October’s housing starts data on November 17.

items._ogDesc: September Canadian inflation breached the BoC target at 3.1%. Regional CPI data reveals only Ontario and BC are below the national average.
items.body:
The August Consumer Price Index (CPI) report breached the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound. Statistics Canada (StatCan) data shows CPI accelerated further in September. A regional breakdown reveals that only two provinces are below the national average. Headline growth is well above the BoC’s target rate, but some provinces have more than doubled that rate.

Canadian Inflation Accelerates, Already Past BoC Upper Bound

Canadian CPI annual growth.

Annual growth of CPI accelerated to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August. The outsized impact of soaring gas prices continues, with CPI ex-gasoline at just 2.2% over the same period. The agency further notes that only 3 of 8 major components saw prices accelerate too.

The headline data makes it easy to conclude this is only an energy story. However, a regional breakdown of CPI makes it clear that basket distortions are in play. Only two provinces have seen a rate lower than the national average.

Atlantic Provinces Over 2x BoC Target, Only 2 Provinces Below Average

Despite being above the Bank of Canada (BoC) upper bound of 3.0%, CPI may be skewed by its modelling. A quick look at the provincial breakdowns, and we see Ontario (+2.5%) is the only province below the threshold. Add BC (+3.0%) to the mix, and we get the only two provinces lower than the national average. The rest of Canada isn’t quite this lucky—especially out east.

CPI’s highest growth is almost exclusively concentrated in Atlantic Canada. PEI’s annual growth of 5.7%—approaching triple the BoC’s target of 2%—is the highest in the country. Not far behind are Nova Scotia (+5.6%), New Brunswick (+5.0%), and Newfoundland and Labrador (+4.7%). The Prairies aren’t much better off either—Manitoba (+4.4%), Alberta (+3.6%), and Saskatchewan (+3.3%) are above the national average too.

It’s not just gas, either. CPI ex-gasoline remained elevated in Nova Scotia (+4.4%), PEI (+3.9%), and New Brunswick (+3.4%). The agency separately notes “… rent prices rose the fastest in Atlantic Canada,” which can help explain some of the distortion.

Energy and Shelter Are Among The Biggest Drivers of CPI

The biggest driver of annual growth remains energy, with 19% annual growth. The sector is driven by a 27.8% surge in gas, along with a 57.8% jump in fuel oil. Considering energy is an input cost for everything, its surprising growth isn’t broad.

Shelter accelerated 1.8%, driven by home/mortgage insurance (+4.9%) and rent (+2.8%). The sector was moderated by falling replacement costs (-1.9%), tied to the cost of building new homes. It was dragged further by mortgage interest (-0.2%), which is likely to be news to brokers considering yields.

In short, Canada’s headline inflation is running hot—and the national average is weak in contrast to what most households are experiencing.

items.title: What Canada's latest inflation reading means for mortgages
items.description: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.content: <p>Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639280340084394431.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Could September’s CPI data impact the BoC’s next decision on October 28?
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate came in at 3.1% last month, a reading that some experts believe could keep the Bank of Canada on hold when it meets next week.

The consumer price index (CPI) climbed slightly over August, according to new Statistics Canada data, but analysts including Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper say the rise likely wasn’t enough to justify an October hike.

“The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting,” Cooper said this morning. “Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent.

“Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Latest inflation reading ‘good news’: economist

A rate hold by the Bank of Canada would mean no change for variable mortgage rates, although five-year Government of Canada bond yields – which heavily influence fixed rates – have continued an unpredictable path and whipsawed over the past five days.

Those yields had ticked slightly higher at time of writing on Monday afternoon compared with the same time yesterday.

Still, National Bank of Canada (NBC) chief economist Stéfane Marion, speaking in a keynote address at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary, described the latest inflation reading as a positive one for the mortgage market.

“Good news this morning – inflation came out, it’s not dramatic,” he said. “Core inflation is still at 2%. I don’t think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking next week, and if they do hike, they can’t be too aggressive.”

CPA Canada chief economist David-Alexandre Brassard also sees the latest reading keeping rate hikes off the table this month. “For now, there is still no clear-cut reason for the Bank of Canada to move interest rates in either direction, as both risks [a weakening economy and rising inflation] are working against one another,” Brassard said.

And he hinted that a further dramatic spike in rates looks unlikely at this stage. “I think most of the increase that we’ve seen in interest rates is behind us,” he said. “And if we’re right, it sets the stage for a normalization going into next year.”

Inflation on the rise, but sluggish economy isn’t picking up

While inflation has been ticking upwards in recent months, the economy has remained sluggish – with some forecasts indicating a further slowdown could be in store.

The Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB), which represents 103,000 small and medium-sized firms, said in its latest Main Street Quarterly report that it sees Canada’s overall GDP growth slowing again in the fourth quarter.

The latest inflation increase was spurred, unsurprisingly, by another surge in fuel oil and other fuel costs, which soared by 57.8% amid continuing price pressures from the war in Iran.

Homeowners’ home and mortgage insurance costs rose by 4.9% compared with the same time last year, while homeowners’ maintenance and repairs costs also moved higher (by 1.2%).

For now, the rate outlook remains uncertain for scores of buyers, particularly with the mortgage renewal wave still going strong.

Speaking with Canadian Mortgage Professional, Haventree Bank president and chief executive officer Fern Glowinsky (pictured below) said mortgage brokers are coming to the fore in that environment.

“I think if there’s a good option in front of the borrower right now for a longer period of time, that’s a good call,” she said. “I think if you can find an offer that lines up with affordability and structure for you that takes you through this period of uncertainty, it’s probably a good idea – because over time, things will settle down.”

items.description: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.content: <p>National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280326776111776.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: National Bank economist calls for foreign buyer ban revision as unsold condos hit a 30-year high
items.body:
With additional reporting by Fergal McAlinden

Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC), has called on the federal government to revise the country’s ban on non-resident foreign homebuyers, arguing the restriction directly undermines Ottawa’s drive to restore Canada’s appeal to international investors.

Speaking at the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary on Tuesday, Marion said he expects Ottawa to act before the ban’s January 1, 2027 expiry — and that any revision should specifically permit foreign nationals to purchase new-build homes.

He framed the call around a striking market figure: 28% of newly constructed condominiums are currently unsold, a level he said is the highest since the early 1990s.

“How can you pretend to be a standout investor again if you tell foreign buyers you can’t touch the residential market in Canada?” Marion said.

“I think they’re going to revise this at a time where 28% of condos that they built are not absorbed, which is the highest proportion we’ve seen since the early 1990s. So against this backdrop, I would certainly expect to see some modification to allow foreigners to buy into new build, and that fits the overall message of making Canada investable again.”

Those views align with a growing chorus across the industry. Don Kottick, president of RE/MAX Canada, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this month that the ban has actively suppressed the very supply the market needs.

“I think if you look at the foreign buyer ban and the negative impact that it had on preconstruction, it took a lot of money out of the market that would have driven more preconstruction, more units coming on the market,” Kottick said.

“So hopefully, if that is removed in January, we start to see more investment coming back, which could drive affordability.” 

Kottick was equally direct on government intervention more broadly. “We’ve had governments that have always tried to bring policy. Policy will never fix the market,” he said.

“Hopefully the government has learned a lesson that natural market forces have been more beneficial than any government policy — because there’s always been unintended consequences.”

The remarks add a prominent voice to a debate that has gathered pace in recent months. Industry pressure for a new-build exemption has been building as the ban’s January 2027 expiry approaches, particularly among developers and pre-sale brokers.

The decision Ottawa makes before year-end ranks among the most consequential housing policy calls it faces in 2026.

Demographic slowdown and the immigration reset

Marion was equally pointed on immigration. Canada moved from roughly 1.2 million newcomers annually at its recent peak to approximately 200,000, a near-collapse in inflows that has weighed heavily on demand across Ontario, British Columbia, and Quebec, where population growth has effectively stalled.

“We went from going to 1.2 million people a year a couple years ago to a dramatic slowdown, just 200,000,” he said.

“At most it’s 300,000 — that’s what the system can cope with. Negative population growth is not the solution either.”

He highlighted Canada’s long-term demographic advantage. The country remains the only jurisdiction globally projecting no population decline through 2066, a structural foundation, he argued, that underpins long-term housing demand even amid near-term disruption.

Broker implications and the 2027 stabilization forecast

Marion projected the national composite index — down 4% in 2026 — to level off by 2027, supported by labour shortages and construction cost pressures that limit the downside.

For brokers, the broader deregulation agenda Marion outlined may prove as relevant as any single housing policy shift.

“I am the most optimistic I’ve been over a decade,” he said.

items.description: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.content: <p>Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280217704442110.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Canada’s top bank economists have weighed in on October 28 after Tuesday’s CPI release
items.body:
Four economists from Canada’s largest financial institutions are calling a Bank of Canada rate hold at the October 28 meeting in Ottawa, after September’s consumer price index (CPI) landed below market consensus and the Bank’s preferred core measures averaged 1.9% year-over-year.

The consensus is patience, but not without a dissenting voice on timing.

What economists are saying about the October 28 rate decision

Leslie Preston, Managing Director and Senior Economist at TD Economics in Canada, set the tone.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September, in contrast to higher inflation south of the border,” she wrote.

“Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year. There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild.” 

Abbey Xu, economist at RBC Economics in Toronto, flagged a more cautious signal from Governor Tiff Macklem himself.

Xu noted that Macklem, speaking at the IMF meetings in Bangkok, warned “the risk that inflation broadens and becomes more persistent has gone up,” and that the Bank has found it increasingly difficult to look through the direct impact of higher energy prices.

RBC’s base case holds the overnight rate at 2.25% through year-end before rising modestly in 2027.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist at CIBC in Toronto, went further, noting that bond yields moved before Tuesday’s release on the back of Macklem’s weekend remarks.

“It’s possible that a first interest rate hike could come earlier than the January move we previously forecast,” he said. 

Dr. Sherry Cooper, Chief Economist at Dominion Lending Centres in Canada, read the September data as confirmation that energy is not yet spreading into broader price growth.

“Today’s inflation report reinforces our view that higher gasoline prices temporarily boost headline inflation while further eroding household purchasing power. However, these energy-driven increases, largely tied to geopolitical tensions, are unlikely to trigger a broader resurgence in underlying inflation,” she said.

On the Bank’s next move, Cooper was direct: “The September data support our base-case scenario that the Bank of Canada will remain on hold at its October 28 meeting. Policymakers will continue to closely monitor incoming inflation data and stand ready to tighten policy if price pressures broaden and become more persistent. Still, for now, underlying inflation trends in Canada remain consistent with a patient, wait-and-see approach.”

Behind the September CPI numbers

Statistics Canada’s September report showed headline CPI at 3.1% year-over-year, above August’s 3.0% but below the 3.2% consensus estimate.

Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year-over-year from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May.

Grocery store prices rose 1.7% year-over-year, the slowest pace since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter inflation ticked to 1.8% from 1.5%, driven by fuel oil costs and higher homeowners’ insurance premiums.

The Bank of Canada’s preferred core gauges — CPI-trim and CPI-median — averaged 1.9% year-over-year, slipping below August’s 2.0% and below the Bank’s own 2% inflation target.

items.title: Ahead Of BC Election, UDI, Housing Central Push For Four Actions
items.description:
On October 13, the Urban Development Institute (UDI), BC Non-Profit Housing Association (BCNPHA), Aboriginal Housing Management Association (AHMA), and Co-operative Housing Federation of BC (CHFBC) — the latter three of which are together known as Housing Central — published a joint news release “calling on every party in the provincial election to commit to bringing down the cost of building homes” as Election Day nears.

UDI is the group that lobbies on behalf of private developers while the Housing Central partners represent the non-profits, Indigenous housing providers, and co-ops in the community housing sector.

Because of their different focuses, the two groups are often on opposite sides of housing debates, hence why they described themselves as “unlikely allies.” They say they are coming together now because they have all reached the same conclusion: “neither sector can build at today’s costs and within an uncertain regulatory and funding environment.”

“The cost of building and financing a home in BC now exceeds what most buyers can afford to pay and what governments are willing to subsidize for low- and moderate-income renters,” the alliance said in their news release. “For market and non-market builders alike, this means projects that don't pencil and never get off the drawing board.”

With Budget 2026 earlier this year, the Province said they were adjusting the pacing of $1.4 billion in planned housing investments, which notably included an abrupt pause pertaining to the Community Housing Fund, which has stranded numerous non-profit housing projects and become a sore spot for the sector.

The groups say over 5,000 affordable rental units have been impacted, and project proponents have lost $45 million in pre-development costs.

After the Governments of Canada and Ontario announced an $8.8 billion deal this spring to cut development charges and eliminate the 13% HST on housing, the development industry in BC started pushing for a similar deal.

While the Governments of Canada and British Columbia finally made an announcement in June, it included a similar deal to cut development charges, but there was nothing on eliminating the GST, with the Province saying they were uninterested in it despite recognizing that the industry had been pushing for it.

In their joint news release, UDI and the Housing Central partners noted that the agreement to reduce development charges was not finalized before Premier David Eby called a snap election on September 22, and thus builders still cannot price it into their projects.

The alliance called for four actions to address the above points:

  1. Restoring the planned investments into non-profit, co-op and Indigenous housing so that the development of 5,000 affordable homes can get back on track.
  2. Finalize a commitment to co-invest remaining BC Rental Protection Funds with the Canada Rental Protection Fund to continue protecting the affordability that already exists in the market and provide housing stability for thousands of tenants across BC.
  3. Finalizing the federal-provincial agreement on development cost charges and infrastructure within [90] days of forming government, so DCC reductions reach projects on the ground.
  4. Following Ontario’s lead by securing a GST exemption on new homes for all buyers, not only first-time buyers.

“The projects are ready, but the land sits empty,” said BCNPHA CEO Jill Atkey. “The people waiting for affordable housing cannot wait another budget cycle. The next government has an opportunity to restore the investment and get these homes built.”

“When market developers and non-profit housing providers are asking for the same thing, it should tell every party how serious the cost of delivery crisis is,” added UDI CEO Mike Drummond.

Housing has not been as front-and-centre compared to the election in 2024, with this election’s primary focuses being Eby’s record and decision to call the election, the economy, and BC’s Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act (DRIPA).

The most substantial commitment on the housing front has been Eby and the NDP’s proposed Unsold Condo Tax on completed unsold inventory, which has drawn widespread criticism from the industry.

Election Day is Saturday, October 24.

items.title: September CPI keeps Bank of Canada hold in play
items.description: Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline
items.content: <p>Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639280143870576555.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Core inflation eases to 1.9% as energy prices drive the headline
items.body:
Canada’s annual inflation rate climbed to 3.1% in September, up from 3.0% in August, according to Statistics Canada data released Monday — and economists say the reading gives the Bank of Canada (BoC) little reason to lift its overnight rate at the October 28 meeting.

Energy drove nearly all of the acceleration. Gasoline prices surged 27.8% year over year, up from 22.8% in August, as crude oil reached its highest level since May amid ongoing Middle East conflict.

Broader energy costs rose 19.0% annually, following a 15.4% gain the prior month. Excluding energy entirely, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose just 2.2%.

Core pressures stay contained

For mortgage brokers advising clients on rate timing, the more instructive signal came from the BoC’s preferred core measures.

CPI-median fell to 1.9% in September from 2.0% in August, while CPI-trim eased to 1.8% from 1.9%, both moving away from hike territory and averaging 1.9% across the two, down from 2.0% the month prior.

Leslie Preston, managing director and senior economist at TD Economics in Toronto, offered a clear verdict.

“No jump scares in Canada’s inflation in September,” she said.

“There is little evidence higher energy costs are bleeding through to broader price pressures, which remain mild. Today’s number supports our view that the Bank of Canada can remain on hold this year.”

That view aligns with analysis from Abbey Xu, economist at Royal Bank of Canada in Toronto, who found limited evidence that elevated energy costs were generating significant second-round inflation in her reading of August’s data, a conclusion September’s numbers do nothing to challenge.

Grocery prices also moderated further. Food purchased from stores rose 1.7% year over year in September, the smallest annual gain since May 2024, down from 2.8% in August.

Shelter prices edged up 1.8%, with rent rising 2.8%.

Don Kottick of RE/MAX Canada says buyers remain willing to make compromises, from relocating farther from city centres to adjusting their spending habits, to achieve their homeownership goals. https://t.co/GOHrsHlsWY — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 14, 2026

What October 28 means for brokers

The September CPI release is the last major data point before the October 28 decision, which will be accompanied by a full Monetary Policy Report.

As CMP reported following Canada’s September labour market shock, a deteriorating jobs picture had already pulled near-term hike expectations sharply lower.

Charles St-Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union in Edmonton, described the Governing Council’s bind plainly.

“We believe it will opt for patience,” he said.

“As a result, we think the BoC will keep its policy rate unchanged for the rest of the year, unless there are signs in the CPI data of a broadening of inflation.”

Dr. Sherry Cooper, chief economist at Dominion Lending Centres (DLC) in Vancouver, pointed directly to Monday’s release: “The Bank of Canada will likely hold off on a rate hike, especially if the inflation data released on October 19 brings no nasty surprises.”

With the overnight rate at 2.25%, held across eight consecutive meetings, mortgage professionals navigating client conversations ahead of the October 28 BoC decision now have their clearest signal yet.

As Leah Zlatkin, a licensed mortgage broker and LowestRates.ca expert, has cautioned: “There’s no clear signal that rates are heading materially lower, and in some cases we’re already seeing lenders adjust pricing upward.” October 28 looks unlikely to change that.

items.title: Down payment rules outdated, says credit union CEO
items.description: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items._ogDesc: Beem's Brian Harris urges greater emphasis on financial behaviour
items.body:
With housing costs and living expenses remaining high in B.C., people struggling to save for a down payment shouldn't be shut out of homeownership, says the CEO of a major credit union.

Brian Harris, president and CEO of Beem Credit Union, said down payments have become an “outdated” primary measure of a person’s readiness for homeownership, an argument that at least one housing expert disputes.

“If you think about the fact that people are saving money anywhere from three to nine years to get into homeownership, that's a lot of money tied up in rental that could have otherwise been much more constructively used,” said Harris.

“I just think it's a really outdated way of determining worthiness and readiness for homeownership.”

About one-third (32 per cent) of Canadians said saving for a down payment was their main barrier to entering the housing market, according to a 2025 survey by CPA Canada and BDO Debt Solutions.

A September survey by Royal LePage also found that more than half of the 1,400 newcomers surveyed across Canada cited saving for a down payment as their biggest barrier for homeownership.

Harris said a family in Metro Vancouver could pay $5,000 a month in rent—an amount that could be comparable to the monthly mortgage payment on a home worth roughly $1 million, depending on the financing terms.

Rather than using down payment as a predominant criterion, Harris said lenders could take a more thoughtful and creative approach to evaluating mortgage applicants by considering their credit history, spending habits and track record of rental payment.

“We have consumer-directed finance, or open banking, as it’s more affectionately referred to, coming to Canada, so we have the ability in the very near term to have really good data insights to determine how somebody is spending their money,” he said.

Canada’s consumer-driven banking framework is designed to allow consumers to share their financial data securely with accredited third-party providers of their choice. The federal government has established the legislative framework and is developing supporting regulations to put it into operation.

“There's a real opportunity for us to use demonstrated behaviours and other sort of support tools to get people in [if] they've exhibited good financial behaviours,” said Harris.

He said a more flexible approach to mortgage qualification could also benefit the broader housing market by matching the demand for homeownership with accessibility.

“I think it's got a lot of great knock-on effects. It gets people who are renting into whatever form it takes, a small home, a condo, a townhouse, whatever it might be,” said Harris.

“But it then also frees up the rental market for those who are not yet ready to buy their own home.”

Down payment requirements still matter

While a down payment is not the only indicator of someone’s readiness for homeownership, removing the requirement could increase risks for both lenders and buyers, according to one real estate expert.

“The benefits of having a down payment, both in terms of an indication that the borrower's capable of making ongoing payments or de-risking the loan for the lender, I think are still true,” said Thomas Davidoff, an associate professor and director for UBC Centre for Urban Economics and Real Estate.

He said one of the main benefits of requesting a down payment is that it makes it harder for the buyer to get to a situation where the property is worth less than what the borrower owes, so they may walk away and stop paying the mortgage.

The ability to save for a down payment remains an important indicator of a person’s capability to save, alongside a good credit history, he said. However, he acknowledged that it is harder than it used to be to save for a down payment due to housing affordability issues in the region.

“If the money comes from the parents, less so, but on the other hand … that indicates you have [supportive] parents, which is helpful,” he said.

A down payment also reduces the amount a buyer needs to borrow, lowering monthly mortgage payments and borrowing costs, Davidoff added.

In addition, the current housing downturn indicates that property prices could fall, making high loan-to-value mortgages riskier, he said.

The key to tackling housing affordability is not in changing mortgage qualification rules, but lies in increasing the supply and growing the economy to boost people’s incomes and purchasing power, according to Davidoff.

“Higher earnings, more houses, that's the recipe,” he said.

“Make sure people are more able to earn a strong income with better education and a stronger labour market, more employers, so things like trade diversification in the face of U.S. tariffs, anything like that helps.”

items.title: The strategic side to alternative lending
items.description: Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate
items.content: <p>Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0343_639257040480876337.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation on why the savviest brokers start with the exit, not the rate
items.body:
Mortgage brokers have no shortage of lender options. More choice should make finding a mortgage solution easier, however, for many brokers, it can have the opposite effect.

Every lender comes with different products, pricing, guidelines, and nuances. Add alternative lenders into the mix, and the challenge isn't just knowing who will fund a deal. It's knowing when to use which option and why.

Private and alternative lending was once seen primarily as a last resort. Today there's a growing opportunity for Mortgage Brokers to leverage this flexibility more strategically to solve timing, preserve favorable existing financing, access equity, or give the client the time they need to reach their next step.

That's an important distinction in alternative lending, where financing may only be needed for a few months, or even a few weeks. For Mortgage Brokers, the real opportunity is understanding what the client is trying to accomplish and then looking at the numbers in that context.

Maybe a real estate investor has found the right property but needs to close quickly. A homeowner could have plenty of equity but needs another year before they're ready to refinance conventionally. Or a client may already have a great first mortgage they don't want to give up but needs access to additional capital.

This is where Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation believes mortgage brokers can bring more strategy to the conversation.

Start with the exit

These aren't necessarily clients who need a permanent alternative mortgage. They may just need the right financing for this particular moment.

This is where starting with the exit becomes critical to the solution. The client’s end goal, how long they need the financing and what needs to happen next should all influence how the deal is structured.

A four-month plan can become six months. A sale can take longer than expected. A refinance can be delayed. Building flexibility into the financing from the start can help keep a temporary solution from becoming an expensive one. When the financing supports the client’s bigger goal, everyone wins: the client has a clearer path forward and the broker builds a relationship that can extend well beyond one deal.

The real cost of financing

Comparing an alternative mortgage rate directly with a conventional rate doesn't always tell the full story. How long the financing is needed, how it's structured and what it allows the client to accomplish all matter.

If financing is only needed for four months, for example, what will it actually cost over those four months? And what could waiting for a lower-rate option mean for the client's plans?

For a real estate investor, moving quickly could mean securing the right property or completing renovations in time to refinance or sell. For a homeowner, short-term financing could bridge the timing gap between buying and selling, or provide the flexibility needed to transition to traditional financing.

Calvert Home Mortgage has built its approach around flexibility, creative problem-solving and strong mortgage broker partnerships, with teams working together to uncover opportunities within a deal, whether that means structuring a blanket mortgage, preserving an existing first mortgage or finding another way to make the numbers work for the client's next step.

Structure can change the numbers too. A client with an attractive first mortgage may be better served by keeping it in place and adding a short-term second rather than refinancing the entire balance. Looking at the blended cost overall can give the mortgage broker and client a much more useful comparison than looking at the second mortgage rate on its own or at refinancing an entire mortgage.

“A good mortgage broker isn’t just finding their client a mortgage for today. They’re thinking about where that client needs to be six months, a year or two years from now,” says Jesse Bobrowski, VP of Growth at Calvert Home Mortgage. “Our role is to work alongside our partners, bring our lending experience to the conversation and help find a path that gets their client where they want to go.”

Putting alternative lending to work

As the real estate and mortgage markets become more challenging, straightforward deals may be harder to come by. For mortgage brokers, that makes the ability to solve more complex needs more valuable.

Using alternative lending strategically doesn’t mean knowing every product or guideline. It means recognizing when a different approach could help and having a lending partner who can work through the options with you.

At Calvert Home Mortgage, we want brokers to bring us the story. What is the client trying to do? What’s getting in the way? And where do they want to go?

“In this market, you’re not going to win every deal with the obvious solution,” says Jesse Bobrowski, VP of Growth at Calvert Home Mortgage Investment Corporation. “Sometimes you need a lender who’s willing to dig in, ask questions and look for another way forward.”

The best mortgage brokers don’t have every answer. They have the right partners to help find one. In a competitive market, that ability to find a way forward is what sets them apart.

items.body:
Time for your cheat sheet on this week’s top stories.

Canadian Real Estate

Canada’s Housing Crash Rivals US In 2008, But The Pain Is Hidden: BMO

The Canadian housing crash now rivals the US in 2008, with prices falling for nearly 5 years. However, unlike the US crash, Canada’s economy appears to have avoided most of the negatives. The country’s economy grew 1.7% annually over the four years, helped by stronger borrowers and rate cuts. Strong headline data is hiding the true impact, warns BMO Capital Markets. That strong GDP growth is actually negative when adjusted per capita. Meanwhile, resilient consumption is due to a reliance on seniors, who aren’t impacted by a rise in unemployment so sharp it’s rarely seen outside of recessions. The economy is in turmoil, the optics are just focused on the wrong areas.

Canadian Real Estate Spent 5 Years Wiping Out Just 13 Months of Gains

Canadian home prices fell 0.9% (-$5.7k) to $651,400 in September, 22.5% (-$189k) lower than the March 2022 peak. Home prices are now down to February 2021 levels, a timeline worth some attention. The painful market correction that’s lasted almost 5 years has only managed to wipe out 13 months of gains. Historically weak sales and near-record high inventory suggest the downturn isn’t over.

Canadian Bond Yields & Borrowing Rates To Rise With US Inflation: BMO

Borrowing in Canada is set to get more expensive due to rising US inflation. Canada’s 2-year government bond yield rose to 3.25% this week, and the Bank of Canada is expected to hike 1 point by 2027. Yields were driven by higher gas prices, but continued to climb even after gas prices stopped. BMO warns Canada’s yields are rising due to US inflation, despite domestic weaknesses.

Canadians Plan To Buy First Home At 41, Property Ladder Breaks: RBC

Canadians plan to enter the housing market at a much later age in life than past generations. A new survey from RBC found the average first-time buyer plans to buy at 41 years old, 12 years later than usual. Being older with higher incomes, they plan to skip starters and want a long-term purchase. At the same time, nearly half of the owners who want to upgrade can’t actually afford to in this market. This combination can mean the end of the property ladder, and a big change for the real estate industry.

items.title: Potential BoC rate hikes loom over Canada’s housing market outlook
items.description: Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO
items.content: <p>Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639278467518790697.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Homebuyers might normally be tempted to enter the market to get ahead of rate increases – but that’s not happening, says Royal LePage CEO
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is still expected to hold rates steady at its next meeting on October 28, but financial markets are pricing in an increasing likelihood that the central bank will start hiking in the months ahead amid continuing concerns about the inflation outlook.

While a sluggish labour market looks set to tip the balance in favour of another BoC hold at the end of the month, experts don’t see that wait-and-see approach lasting for long.

Dominion Lending Centres Group (DLCG) chief economist Sherry Cooper suggested a rate increase could arrive as soon as December 9, the Bank’s last scheduled rate decision of the year, as global pressure gathers for central banks to take a more aggressive stand on inflation.

The BoC’s benchmark rate, which strongly influences variable Canadian mortgage rates, has remained unchanged throughout the year to date. But fixed rates have been climbing in recent weeks, reflecting jitters in global bond markets and adding further complications for mortgage shoppers.

A rate increase by the US Federal Reserve in its last decision also sparked speculation that Canada’s central bank could be set to follow suit soon.

Rising rates are tempering already subdued expectations for the housing market. On Friday, the Canadian Real Estate Association (CREA) slashed its 2026 home sales forecast for the third consecutive quarter, while TD has also revised its own outlook.

Why potential homebuyers aren’t pushing ahead

The looming possibility of Bank of Canada rate hikes might sometimes spur potential homebuyers into action because their borrowing costs could be much higher if they wait for a few months.

Amid the current economic uncertainty, that doesn’t appear to be the case, according to Royal LePage president and chief executive officer Phil Soper (pictured top). He told Canadian Mortgage Professional that would-be buyers still appear to prefer sitting on the sidelines because they’re nervous about the US-Canada trade war and rising inflation.  

“You’d expect with lots of chatter about rate increases in Canada online bubbling through communities – plus the recent significant rise in fixed-rate mortgages in the United States – that there’d be some pull-ahead in activity,” Soper said. “You’d see some people that were planning to get into the market in the spring of 2027, for example, jumping in now to get ahead of anticipated higher borrowing costs.

“Yet we’re not seeing material changes in the trajectory of transaction volumes. It’s very flat. And what that says to me is even an incentive like that is not enough to get people off the sidelines if they’re feeling very uncomfortable.”

Soper: Fundamentals in place for healthy market, but Canadians remain nervous

Royal LePage now expects a more modest pace of national 2026 home price growth than it first anticipated. In its second-quarter house price survey, the real estate firm said prices would likely jump by 2% by Q4 – but it’s revised that to 1%, reflecting the deep freeze that still grips the market.

Major markets including Toronto and Vancouver saw prices continue to slide in the second quarter, according to Royal LePage, although other cities including Montreal bucked the national trend.

Soper suggested meaningful change in the housing market outlook might not arrive unless positive news emerges on the trade war, which has seen the US and Canada exchange a flurry of tariffs and counter-tariffs on products crossing the border.

“It doesn’t seem that anything will budge Canadians from their rigor mortis while this trade war is raging with the United States,” he said. “What I mean by that is we’ve got pent-up demand, we’ve got reasonable mortgage rates, we’ve got lower home prices, employment’s reasonable and steady, and savings are high.

“All the fundamentals are in place for a much more active housing market, but our research shows first-time homebuyers in particular are just so nervous about the trade war, and in particular Donald Trump’s behaviour and what it might mean to Canada and ultimately to them, that they are sitting on the sidelines and waiting.”
